tldr: This paper introduces ESRP, an embodied AI task where an agent must rearrange furniture into a target configuration using only an egocentric camera view and a single top-down floor plan. Testing state-of-the-art RL, VLMs, and classical planning methods across more than 5,400 realistic scenes in OmniGibson revealed a peak success rate of only around 30%, highlighting long-horizon spatial planning under partial observability as an open and extremely difficult frontier.
hero_caption: Overview of the ESRP task. Using only a top-down view of the target room layout (top right) and its own egocentric camera view, the robot sequentially moves furniture from the initial configuration (red) to the target configuration (green). Without access to a global map or ground-truth localization, the agent must infer the overall space from partial visual observations and perform long-horizon planning.
overview:
If you ask a human to rearrange a room, showing them a single floor plan of the finished layout is usually enough for them to plan out the steps: "Move this sofa over there first, then bring this chair here." However, prior research in Embodied AI has largely focused on tabletop rearrangement of small objects like cups, or on 2D planar simulations where ground-truth object locations and obstacle maps are fully visible from the start. When moving large furniture in a real room, an agent cannot see the whole space from its camera alone, and it faces mutual object occlusions as well as complex physical constraints—such as needing to clear a chair before a table can pass through.

To tackle this, the authors introduce a novel task called ESRP (Embodied Scene Rearrangement Planning), where the agent must rearrange furniture using only egocentric RGB images and a single top-down target layout. They also build ESRP-Bench, a large-scale benchmark on the realistic physics simulator OmniGibson, incorporating over 5,400 indoor scenes and more than 8,200 pieces of furniture derived from the 3D-FRONT dataset.

To evaluate this challenge, they thoroughly benchmark four distinct baselines: imitation learning (Diffusion Policy), reinforcement learning (PPO), a modern vision-language model approach (ReAct with a VLM), and a task-and-motion planning (TAMP) baseline that is granted privileged global information.

The results show that even TAMP with complete global knowledge achieves a success rate of only 30.20%, and all baselines drop to near 0% success in difficult scenes with four or more movable objects. Notably, over 60% of all failures occur not during finding or transporting objects, but at the placement stage—releasing the furniture accurately into the target location. This highlights that long-horizon spatial understanding and precise placement under partial observability remain a formidable hurdle for current embodied agents.
contributions: Defined ESRP, a realistic and challenging new task of rearranging furniture using only egocentric RGB observations and a top-down target layout.
Constructed ESRP-Bench on OmniGibson, featuring over 5,400 scenes and 8,200 objects, along with three multi-level evaluation metrics.
Provided a comprehensive comparison across four paradigms—imitation learning, reinforcement learning, VLMs, and a privileged TAMP planner—identifying key bottlenecks in current embodied AI.

sections.heading: Rearranging Real Furniture from an Egocentric Perspective
sections.summary: Prior rearrangement work focused on tabletop manipulation or 2D planar simplifications with omniscient views. This paper introduces ESRP, a realistic task of moving furniture in 3D space using only first-person views and a top-down goal image, alongside its benchmark, ESRP-Bench.
sections.details:
Research on robotic scene rearrangement has traditionally branched into two main directions. One is tabletop manipulation using robotic arms to organize small everyday objects. Because these tasks take place in a confined workspace, they do not require room-scale navigation or global spatial reasoning. The other direction involves room-scale rearrangement, but these setups often simplify the world into 2D planes or grant the robot full global ground-truth states from the beginning. Such assumptions do not hold in real-world 3D environments where large furniture constantly obstructs the agent's field of view.

To bridge this gap, the authors formulate ESRP (Embodied Scene Rearrangement Planning). The agent receives only egocentric RGB images from its own camera and a single top-down layout depicting the target configuration. This setup presents three core challenges:

- Partial observability: The agent must mentally align its narrow egocentric view with the global target map and infer unobserved areas.
- Inter-object dependencies: Moving large objects demands deadlock prevention and strict ordering, such as having to move object B before placing object A.
- Dynamically changing environments: Every moved piece of furniture alters the room's traversable areas and sightlines, constantly changing localization and navigation conditions.

To tackle this problem, the authors developed ESRP-Bench on OmniGibson and established baselines spanning imitation learning, reinforcement learning, VLMs, and classical planning to evaluate current limitations.

sections.heading: What Fundamentally Sets This Apart from Prior Rearrangement and TAMP Work?
sections.summary: Existing rearrangement studies were limited to tabletop setups or 2D simplifications, while TAMP methods struggle with long horizons and complex 3D geometry. This work sets itself apart by combining a full 3D physics environment with the practical constraint of an egocentric viewpoint.
sections.details:
Reviewing related work highlights the unique position of this paper.

In the context of rearrangement planning, significant progress has been made on tabletop manipulation tasks, such as clearing dishes or sorting blocks. These works achieve strong results using sampling-based planning or reinforcement learning, but they do not scale to room-wide mobile rearrangement. While some room-scale studies handle furniture, they often treat obstacles as 2D polygons and assume an unrealistic global overhead view of the entire room. This omits height constraints, 3D geometry, and the visual occlusions inherent to the physical world.

In Task and Motion Planning (TAMP), which combines high-level discrete sequencing with low-level continuous trajectory generation, existing methods struggle when search spaces explode over long horizons or when complex 3D geometry is involved. Furniture rearrangement requires simultaneous geometric and sequential reasoning: calculating clearances based on furniture dimensions so the robot can pass, and figuring out which piece to move first to avoid deadlocks.

ESRP overcomes these simplifications by serving as a benchmark that simultaneously challenges agents with an egocentric viewpoint, full 3D physical interactions, and long planning horizons.

sections.heading: Inside ESRP-Bench: Task Formulation, Dataset, and Four Baselines
sections.summary: Built on OmniGibson, ESRP-Bench is a comprehensive testbed with 5,495 scenes and 8,213 objects. It formally defines observation and action spaces, introduces multi-level metrics (SR, OSR, RDR), and implements four diverse baselines across IL, RL, VLMs, and TAMP.
sections.details:
Here is a closer look at the components of the benchmark.

### Task Definition and Simulation Setup
At each step, the robot receives three observations:
- A $128\times 128$ egocentric RGB image $I^{ego}$
- A $128\times 128$ top-down target RGB image $I^{g}$
- A binary flag indicating whether an object is currently grasped, $g \in \{0, 1\}$

The action space consists of six discrete actions: move forward, move backward, turn left ($22.5^\circ$), turn right ($22.5^\circ$), fetch, and release. Translation steps are 0.25m. To focus evaluation on high-level planning, grasping is abstracted using a magic snapping mechanism that attaches an object if it lies within a 1.0m radius of the robot center. However, 3D mesh collisions between the robot, furniture, and walls are strictly simulated by the physics engine.
A task is successful if the 2D bounding box Intersection over Union (IoU) on the horizontal plane between every target object and its goal location exceeds 0.3.

### Dataset Construction
Using the high-quality 3D-FRONT indoor dataset, the authors constructed 5,495 scenes spanning 24 room types, containing 8,213 movable furniture items. Scenes are categorized into three difficulty tiers based on object count: Easy (1 object), Medium (2–3 objects), and Hard (4–6 objects).
Initial configurations were generated using reverse simulation: starting from the target layout, a rule-based agent moved furniture backward to random, collision-free locations. This guarantees that initial states are physically solvable and allows the reversed execution traces to serve directly as expert demonstrations for imitation learning.

### Multi-Level Evaluation Metrics
Performance is evaluated using three metrics:
- SR (Success Rate): The proportion of episodes where all target objects are successfully placed at their goal locations.
- OSR (Object Success Rate): The fraction of individual objects successfully placed across all episodes.
- RDR (Relative Distance Reduction): The ratio of remaining distance to the initial total distance from targets (closer to 0 is better).

### Four Baseline Methods
The authors implemented representative approaches from different paradigms:
- ESRP-BC (Imitation Learning): A Diffusion Policy trained on expert trajectories. It predicts an 8-step future action sequence via a denoising process conditioned on observation history and the goal image.
- ESRP-PPO (Reinforcement Learning): Consists of a ResNet encoder, a single-layer LSTM, and an MLP policy, trained for approximately 6 million steps with PPO. It uses dense rewards for approaching goals and placing objects successfully.
- ESRP-VLM (Foundation Model): Employs a pre-trained VLM (Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct) using ReAct prompting to interleave reasoning and action selection zero-shot without fine-tuning.
- ESRP-PLAN (TAMP): A classical planner granted privileged global state information, knowing the map and all ground-truth object poses. It plans object moving orders exhaustively and generates collision-free paths using Breadth-First Search (BFS) and A* search.

sections.heading: Experimental Results: Even the Best Planner Hits Only 30%, and More Furniture Causes Total Collapse
sections.summary: On the test set, the privileged TAMP planner achieved the highest SR at 30.20%, but all methods plummeted to near 0% as the number of objects increased. Failure analysis revealed that over 60% of failures occurred during object placement rather than navigation or grasping.
sections.details:
Evaluating the baselines on the test set (10% unseen scenes) revealed several key insights.

### Overall Performance and Paradigm Characteristics
Across the board, the privileged ESRP-PLAN achieved the highest overall performance (SR: 30.20%, OSR: 37.19%). Having access to the global room layout and obstacle maps allowed it to generate reliable paths. Conversely, this also demonstrates that even an omniscient planner succeeds only about 30% of the time, underscoring the tight geometric constraints and ordering complexities of the task.

Among the learning-based approaches, ESRP-PPO (SR: 19.33%) slightly outperformed ESRP-BC (SR: 18.04%). In terms of RDR, PPO achieved 0.9416, whereas BC degraded to 1.3418. BC suffered from compounding errors over long horizons, sometimes driving furniture further away from the goal.

The zero-shot ESRP-VLM (Qwen3-VL-2B) achieved an SR of 17.64%. Switching to a more capable backbone, Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite, boosted SR to 23.01%. However, it still did not significantly pull ahead of PPO, showing that general-purpose VLM pre-training alone struggles to solve long-horizon spatial rearrangement.

### Breakdown by Difficulty and Failure-Mode Analysis
While baselines attained 40% to 60% SR in the Easy tier (1 object), performance collapsed entirely to between 0.00% and 0.20% SR in the Hard tier (4–6 objects). Adding more furniture causes combinatorial explosion in task ordering, and moved objects often become new obstacles that trap the agent.

A failure-mode decomposition analyzing whether episodes failed during Navigation (Stage 1), Grasping (Stage 2), or Goal Placement (Stage 3) revealed a striking pattern. Over 60% of all failures were concentrated in Stage 3: 60.85% for PPO, 62.85% for BC, and 66.55% for VLM. Agents can reliably find and grasp furniture, but precisely matching an egocentric viewpoint to a top-down goal map to release the item within target tolerances proves exceptionally difficult.

The robot finds the specified furniture (e.g., chair or stool) without hesitation and delivers it accurately to the target position.

In scenes with 2 objects (top row) or 4 objects (bottom row), mutual inter-object occlusions and long planning horizons prevent the agent from placing objects into precise target poses within the step limit, even if it brings them close.

sections.heading: Conclusion and Future Outlook: Steps Toward Real-World Deployment
sections.summary: This study introduces the practical challenge of egocentric furniture rearrangement, accompanied by a benchmark and baseline analysis. By exposing the limits of current methodologies, it offers an important roadmap for embodied AI research.
sections.details:
This paper presented ESRP, a novel task for rearranging 3D indoor furniture using only egocentric RGB views and a single floor plan layout, alongside the ESRP-Bench benchmark. Testing state-of-the-art RL, VLMs, and classical TAMP across more than 5,400 diverse scenes provided empirical proof of how difficult long-horizon spatial reasoning and precise placement remain under partial observability.

The authors also outline several avenues for future work. The current setting is restricted to room-scale rearrangement and relies exclusively on RGB inputs. Future directions include scaling up to house-scale environments that demand multi-room navigation, as well as incorporating multimodal sensor modalities such as depth maps, Bird's-Eye-View (BEV) representations, or LiDAR point clouds.

As a stepping stone toward deploying assistive robots in smart homes and eldercare, this benchmark provides a valuable catalyst for the embodied AI community.

takeaways: Conditioning an agent on a single top-down goal layout alongside egocentric views mimics natural human instructions and serves as an excellent benchmark for spatial reasoning in embodied AI.
The primary bottleneck for current agents is not object search or navigation, but achieving millimeter-level precision during placement under partial observability.

Even cutting-edge VLMs (such as Gemini) face clear limits in zero-shot spatial planning; resolving complex, long-horizon physical constraints will require explicit geometric representations and dedicated memory structures.
limitations: Grasping is abstracted via magic snapping within a 1.0m radius, setting aside the low-level physical control challenges real robots face when manipulating heavy furniture.
The benchmark is restricted to room-scale environments and does not yet address house-scale planning, where agents must transport furniture across multiple rooms.
Observations are limited strictly to egocentric RGB images, leaving open how performance would change with standard real-robot inputs like depth sensors or SLAM point clouds.
